lead: Don't use everything you know now to insist someone should have known it back then.
when: When something has gone wrong and you need to sort out responsibility, or when you keep blaming yourself with "I should have known," this model offers a different angle.
body:
The name can be misleading. It doesn't refer to a perfectly logical, self-interested person. It means a reasonable, careful person, and what such a person would usually notice and do in that particular situation at that time. It doesn't demand that people never make mistakes.

In law, the reasonable person standard is an objective benchmark used to judge what actions or precautions a reasonably prudent person in the same situation would take.

Think of it as a pair of glasses that take you back to the scene: what information was available then? What risks were obvious? Did this person take the care they should have? That way you don't blame someone just because things went wrong, and nobody gets to dodge real responsibility with "well, I didn't know."
example:
A friend asks you to look after their pet for a few days and tells you about the food, the water, and the window that must stay closed. You follow the instructions, but a small problem comes up with no warning signs at all. That's a very different situation from knowing the window was open and ignoring it completely.

When you assess what happened, you can't just look at whether something went wrong in the end. You also need to look at what could reasonably have been foreseen and whether the right precautions were taken. This makes looking back fairer: fix the process where the process needs fixing, and own up to carelessness where there was carelessness.
extra: Years ago you chose your college major based on a short course description, and only later discovered you didn't actually like it. You can learn from that to ask around more thoroughly next time, but you don't have to expect your 18-year-old self to have had the knowledge you gained over the next ten years.
steps: First reconstruct what was known at the time, leaving out anything that only came to light later.
Ask what a conscientious, responsible person in the same position would usually have checked.
Separate ordinary uncertainty from avoidable carelessness, then talk about how to improve.
caution: This isn't "most people cut corners, so I can too," and it doesn't expect everyone to act like an expert. The actual legal rules are their own matter. Here it's just a way to help you look at people's actions fairly.
exercise: Think of a decision you still regret. Make two columns: "what I knew then" and "what I only learned later." See whether you've been counting everything in the second column as a mistake you made at the time.
brief: A comparison of reasonable care in the same situation: two ordinary stick figures face the same slippery floor and staircase. One sets out a bright warning cone with no text and walks slowly holding the handrail; the other runs and slips.
